summary.text: Invertebrates are animals that neither develop nor retain a vertebral column, the spine or backbone.
The majority of animal species are invertebrates, and one estimate puts the figure at 97%.
The word is a convenience, since some so-called invertebrates, such as tunicates, are more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: From 10 micrometre myxozoans to 10 metre squid

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Latin vertebra, a joint, with in- meaning not

items.prompt: A tunicate has no backbone, yet it is more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates. What does that show about the word invertebrate?

options.label: It names a true branch of animals that all share a recent ancestor
It groups animals by a missing trait, so it is a term of convenience rather than a true branch
It proves that tunicates were wrongly counted among animals
It shows that backbones evolved separately in every animal group

items.explain: Because some invertebrates are closer kin to vertebrates, the grouping is paraphyletic, and the term is one of convenience, not a taxon.

items.prompt: Grouping animals as winged or wingless puts insects, bats and birds together. What weakness does grouping animals by having no backbone share with that?

options.label: Both groupings leave out most of the animals alive today
Both groupings are too small to be of any practical use
Both groupings depend on size rather than on body features
The shared trait does not point to a clear common biological origin for the group

items.explain: The backbone distinction is one of convenience and is not based on any clear biologically homologous trait, much as having wings does not unite insects, bats and birds.

items.prompt: A garden worm has no bones and no hard shell, yet it holds its shape. What gives it a body structure?

options.label: A small internal bone running along its length
A hard outer shell like the ones beetles have
A fluid-filled body that works as a hydrostatic skeleton
A stiff spine that it grows in place of a backbone

items.explain: Many invertebrates, such as worms and jellyfish, have fluid-filled hydrostatic skeletons, while others have hard exoskeletons.

items.prompt: A snail's shell winds around in a spiral. What does that tell you about its body plan?

options.label: It has no symmetry, as is true of every gastropod
It has radial symmetry, like a wheel
It has spherical symmetry, like a ball
It has bilateral symmetry, with matching left and right sides

items.explain: Most body plans show some symmetry, but a minority show none. All gastropods are asymmetric, easily seen in snails with helical shells.

items.prompt: A male fiddler crab loses its oversized claw. What happens after he next moults?

options.label: He grows the large claw back on the same side
He grows a new large claw on the opposite side
He stays with one small claw for the rest of his life
He grows two large claws of equal size

items.explain: Fiddler crabs often have one claw much larger than the other, and a male that loses the large one grows another on the opposite side after moulting.

items.prompt: An invertebrate cannot live on sunlight and water alone. Why not?

options.label: Its lack of a backbone stops it from absorbing light
Only animals with a skeleton are able to digest food
As an animal, it is a heterotroph and must eat other organisms
It makes its own food but too slowly to live on

items.explain: Being animals, invertebrates are heterotrophs and need sustenance from consuming other organisms.
